questions.q: A Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attack works by:
options: Flooding a target server with traffic from many compromised machines
questions.solution: A botnet of 'zombie' systems swamps the target with requests so genuine users cannot be served. Nothing is encrypted (ransomware) or stolen directly - availability alone is attacked.

questions.q: Which of the following is a markup language rather than a programming language?
questions.solution: HTML (HyperText Markup Language) only structures and presents content using tags; it has no logic/control-flow constructs of its own, so it is a markup language. Python, C++ and Java are programming languages.
questions.shortcut: Markup = tags for layout (HTML, XML, Markdown). If the option 'structures web pages', it is not a programming language.

questions.q: Which of the following areas characterises fifth-generation computers?
questions.solution: The 5th generation targets AI, natural-language processing, parallel and quantum-style computing. Punched cards belong to the pre-1st/1st era, assembly is a 2nd-generation language habit, and vacuum tubes are 1st generation.
questions.shortcut: Anything with 'intelligence, learning, robotics, parallel' = 5th generation.

questions.q: The default port number for HTTPS traffic is:
questions.solution: HTTPS runs over TLS on port 443; 80 is plain HTTP, 21 is FTP control, 8080 is a common alternate proxy port.

questions.q: In the passage, the word 'redundant' most nearly means:
questions.solution: Critics believed the internet had made 'buildings full of books redundant' — that is, unnecessary, a thing whose job was over; the next sentence confirms the sense ('The prediction has aged badly' — the prediction of no-longer-needed). (b) cost is never linked to the word; (c) plays on 'duplicate copies', which the passage does not discuss; (d) is the opposite of what critics claimed.
questions.shortcut: Antonym/synonym-in-context: plug your own word ('unnecessary') into the sentence first, then match; ignore options sharing nearby letters or images.

questions.q:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them contains an error. Select the part that contains the error.

I will inform you / as soon as the results / will be declared / by the board.
questions.solution: In a time clause introduced by *as soon as*, the simple present is used for future meaning: *as soon as the results **are declared***. *will be declared* is wrong.

questions.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

One who can use both hands with equal ease
questions.solution: Ambi = both + dextr = right hand/skill → **ambidextrous**. *Ambivalent* means having mixed feelings, *amphibious* means living on land and water — the ambi-/amphi- family tempts, the dextr root decides.

questions.q: According to the passage, librarians these days:
options: spend more time enforcing silence than helping visitors
help residents with official paperwork and online services as much as with books
are replaced by coding clubs in side rooms
questions.solution: Para 2 states: 'Librarians now spend as much time helping residents access government forms and digital services as they do recommending books' — (b) is a direct paraphrase. (a) invents enforcement duties. (c) flips 'as much time... as' into abandonment of books. (d) confuses the location (clubs *use* a side room) with staff replacement.
questions.shortcut: Match the balance in the sentence: 'as much X as Y' means both continue — options that delete either half are wrong.

questions.q: Sarnath was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in —
questions.solution: Sarnath — where the Buddha preached his first sermon — was designated a World Heritage Site on 25 July 2026.

questions.q: A 100 W bulb glows for 10 hours. How much electrical energy does it consume?
questions.solution: Energy = power × time = 100 W × 10 h = 1,000 Wh = **1 kWh** (1 unit).

questions.q: The Urdu weekly ***Al-Hilal*** (1912) was started by —
questions.solution: **Maulana Abul Kalam Azad** launched *Al-Hilal* from Calcutta in 1912. Mohammad Ali Jauhar edited *Comrade*.

questions.q: Which of the following is a rabi crop?
questions.solution: **Mustard** is sown in October–November and harvested in March–April, so it is a **rabi** crop, like wheat, barley and gram. Paddy, jute and cotton are monsoon-sown **kharif** crops.
questions.shortcut: Winter-sown = rabi; the other three need monsoon water.

questions.q:
Sales (in ₹ hundreds) of four shops in a month:

| Shop | A | B | C | D |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sales | 250 | 300 | 400 | 350 |

The total sales of all four shops (in ₹) is:
questions.shortcut: Sum 1300, remember the ×100 unit: ₹1,30,000. Trap: 1300 (forgot the unit).

questions.q: Find the value of $\sqrt{248 + \sqrt{52 + \sqrt{144}}}$.
A path 7 m wide runs around a circular park of radius 14 m. The area of the path is: [Use $\pi=\frac{22}{7}$]
questions.solution:
Outer radius $=14+7=21$ m.

Path area $=\frac{22}{7}(21^2-14^2)=\frac{22}{7}\times245=770$ sq m.

questions.q: What is the smallest number which, when divided successively by 3, 5 and 7, leaves remainders 2, 3 and 4 respectively?
questions.solution:
Work backwards. Last quotient = 0, so the number before division by 7 is 4.
Before division by 5: $5 \times 4 + 3 = 23$.
Before division by 3: $3 \times 23 + 2 = 71$.
Check: $71 = 3 \times 23 + 2$, $23 = 5 \times 4 + 3$, $4 = 7 \times 0 + 4$ ✓.

questions.q: A square sheet is divided into four equal vertical strips. Only the left-most strip is folded over onto the strip next to it. Then three holes are punched: two in the double-layered strip and one in the right half of the sheet (single layer). How many holes are there after unfolding?
questions.solution: The two punches in the covered strip go through 2 layers → 2 × 2 = 4 holes. The punch in the single-layer region → 1 hole. Total **5**.
questions.shortcut: Double only what the flap covers.

questions.q: Find the next term: **12, 13, 21, 48, 112, ?**
questions.solution: Differences: 1, 8, 27, 64 — perfect **cubes**. Next difference 5³ = 125. 112 + 125 = **237**.
questions.shortcut: The moment the ladder reads 1, 8, 27, 64 you are done — add 125.

questions.q: In a certain code, **FORM** is written as **NQPE**. How is **SALT** written in that code?
questions.solution: FORM backwards = MROF; then +1, −1, +1, −1 → NQPE ✓. SALT backwards = TLAS; +1, −1, +1, −1 → **UKBR**.
questions.shortcut: Reverse first, then the alternating shift — the sample's first code letter N = M+1 comes from the last letter M, which proves the reversal came first.

questions.q:
**Statements:** Some numbers are letters. All letters are symbols. No symbol is a digit.

**Conclusions:** I. Some numbers are not digits. II. All letters are digits.
questions.solution: A number-letter element is a letter → symbol → never a digit → I follows. II collides head-on with 'No symbol is a digit' → fails. **Only I.**
questions.shortcut: One shared element propagated through three statements settles I.
